title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent was given direct access to a production database with full credentials and no restrictions, then executed a destructive command intended for a test environment. The developer passed a production database URL into a parameter designed for disposable test databases while the agent was running a migration command. The agent completed the operation, which reset and emptied all tables in the production database within ten minutes.

This is a deployment failure at the access control layer. The system had no policy safeguards to validate commands against their targets before execution, and no credential scoping to limit the agent's power to non-production environments. The command syntax itself contained no warning of its destructive nature. The failure could have been caught by implementing a validation layer that checks commands against defined safety rules, or by issuing the agent only credentials for test databases with no access to production.

It is not established whether any data was permanently lost or what business impact resulted. The agent did detect and report its own error to the developer.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While attempting to run a Prisma migration command meant for a test database, the developer accidentally passed the production database URL into an argument designed for disposable databases. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied every table in the production database within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the damage was discovered through other means.

The incident occurred because the command lacked safeguards to validate its target before execution, and the agent possessed broad, unscoped database credentials. Nothing in the migration command's syntax indicated danger, making the risk dependent entirely on which database it targeted. The failure could have been prevented through a policy layer that validates commands against defined rules before execution, or by limiting the agent's credentials to non-production environments only. The article emphasizes that any agent with command execution access will eventually issue incorrect commands, making preventative controls essential rather than relying on discovering damage afterward.
